title: Pied beauty
hook: a Jesuit thanks God for freckles and fickle things, then ends on a beauty past change (Pied Beauty)
tomorrow: a falcon hangs on the wind. why is the priest's heart hiding?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sweeping as prayer: Herbert's clause, for thy sake, the stone that turns a chore to gold. Herbert's done. Today, another priest, and a stranger poem.

Phone filters smooth every freckle off a face. A Jesuit priest named Gerard Manley Hopkins went the other way. His poem opens like a church prayer: "Glory be to God for dappled things". Then it thanks God for skies patched like a cow's hide, the spots on a trout, finches' wings, and, stranger still, for "Whatever is fickle, freckled (who knows how?)". Fickle? Who thanks God for fickle? And why does a poem crammed with things that keep changing end on someone who doesn't change at all?
screen: `NO MORE FRECKLES.` → `GLORY BE TO GOD FOR DAPPLED THINGS.` → `FICKLE, FRECKLED.` → `WHY END ON WHAT DOESN'T CHANGE?`

segments.voice: Start with his training. Hopkins was a Jesuit, a member of the order whose motto is to the greater glory of God. Jesuits are trained through the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola, and the Exercises begin with a foundation: people are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and the other things on the face of the earth are made to help them. Hopkins looked hard at those other things. In his journals he used his own word, inscape, for the pattern that makes each thing itself and nothing else. Now the puzzle solves itself. The trout gives glory by being spotted. The finch, by its wings. Even the odd ones, in his words "All things counter, original, spare, strange", give glory by being exactly what they are. Then the turn: "He fathers-forth whose beauty is past change: / Praise him." All the changing, freckled things come from a beauty that doesn't change. The poem opens on glory and closes on praise, and some readers hear the old Jesuit habit of writing praise to God at the top and the bottom of a page. That's the Catholic teaching under it: creation itself gives glory to God, and a creature praises by being what it was made to be. It's a roomy idea. Nothing has to be smoothed out first. The freckle is part of the praise.
screen: `A JESUIT: TO THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.` · `IGNATIUS: MADE TO PRAISE.` · `INSCAPE: WHAT MAKES A THING ITSELF.` · `HE FATHERS-FORTH: PRAISE HIM.` · then, large: `DAPPLED THINGS.`

segments.voice: Find one dappled thing within reach: a leaf, a wood grain, a speckled stone, the back of your own hand. For two minutes, look at it the way Hopkins looked, every spot and streak and edge. Let it be exactly what it is. The poem's last two words are there for anyone who wants them: praise him.
Pied beauty: Hopkins's title for the patched, spotted, mixed-up beauty of the world. Pied means patched in more than one color, and for him every patch gives glory.
Pocket this one: dappled things, every spot of them part of the praise. See you tomorrow.
